desc:
The array nums contains only 0 and 1. Cut it into consecutive, non-empty blocks so that every block contains exactly one 1. Every element must belong to some block.

Return the number of different ways to cut the array, modulo 1,000,000,007. Two ways differ if they place a cut at different positions. If no valid cutting exists, return 0.

nums = [0,1,0,0,1]  -> 3   ([0,1 | 0,0,1], [0,1,0 | 0,1], [0,1,0,0 | 1])
nums = [0,1,0]      -> 1   (the whole array)
nums = [0,0]        -> 0   (there is no 1 at all)
hints: Every block holds exactly one 1, so the number of blocks equals the number of 1s. What does that say about the zeros before the first 1 and after the last 1?
Look at two neighbouring 1s with some zeros between them. Exactly one cut must be placed somewhere between them. How many places can it go?
If the neighbouring 1s are at indices a < b, the cut can go in any of b - a gaps. The cuts for different pairs are independent, so multiply these numbers (modulo 1,000,000,007).
editorial: Each block owns one 1, so there is one block per 1, and the zeros before the first 1 or after the last 1 simply join the first or last block (no choice there). Between two consecutive 1s at indices a and b there must be exactly one cut, and it can be placed in any of the b - a gaps between index a and index b.

The choices for different pairs do not influence each other, so the answer is the product of b - a over all neighbouring pairs of 1s, or 0 if the array has no 1. The same result comes from a prefix DP: ways[i] counts the cuttings of the first i elements, and each new 1 multiplies the count by the distance to the previous 1. One pass, O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
